content.title: Michigan overwhelms Alabama to end Tide’s season in Sweet 16: Analysis and notes
content.text: Alabama fought and played like a team who didn’t want to go home, but Michigan eventually played like the No. 1 seed it is. As the NCAA tournament Sweet 16 game progressed, the Wolverines outshot and outmuscled an outmatched Crimson Tide squad. As a result, Michigan defeated No. 4 seed Alabama 90-77 at United Center in Chicago. “There’s a reason they’re a 1-seed,” Alabama coach Nate Oats said. “They’re big, strong, athletic, physical. I thought our guys did a great job to be up two. Did a great job closing the first half. But you know, the start of that second half wasn’t what we were looking for and they kind of imposed their will on us to start the second half.”The Crimson Tide’s season ends with a 25-10 record. Here are notes and analysis from the Sweet 16 matchup between Alabama and Michigan:Labaron Philon battles in first halfThe Crimson Tide’s star guard from Mobile played out of his mind in the first half. Michigan plastered him and suffocated him, but he didn’t let that stop him. He willed Alabama to stay in the game with the Wolverines before the break. The Crimson Tide held a lead most of the first half, but Michigan went on a 14-3 run in the final minutes before halftime. The Wolverines took a 47-41 lead with 1:58 left as a result. Then Philon took over. Alabama went on an 8-0 run to close the half. More accurately, Philon went on an 8-0 run to close the half. He made all six free throws he attempted and a layup. He put Alabama up 49-47 at the break, having scored 19 points, grabbed five boards, tallied three assists and zero turnovers over 19 minutes in the first half. “We played well, went on a little run, and then finished, just completely butchered, the last two minutes of the first half,” Michigan coach Dusty May said. Alabama didn’t even shoot that well against Michigan before the break — 39% for the Crimson Tide compared to 50% for the Wolverines. And yet, Alabama found a way to hold a lead going into the locker room, in large part thanks to Philon.Philon finished the game with 35 points, seven rebounds, and only one turnover over 39 minutes in what is likely his last game with the Crimson Tide. He’s an almost-certain first-round NBA draft pick this summer. Michigan wears down Alabama on the glassThe Crimson Tide, for all its rebounding struggles this season, actually fared better than the Wolverines early in that department. At the first timeout, Alabama held a 7-3 lead in boards with a 4-1 edge on offense. With Michigan’s size and strength, the Crimson Tide wasn’t going to be able to win on the glass for too long. By halftime, the Wolverines held a 21-20 edge on the glass. Then Michigan dominated after the break, winning the rebounding battle 26-12 in the second half. “We ran into a buzz saw the second half,” Oats said. “We couldn’t rebound with them.”Yaxel Lendeborg, in particular, proved imposing. The former UAB star shined as a scorer and rebounder for the Wolverines while also creating offense for his teammates and forcing Alabama into some turnovers. He showed why he’s one of the best players in the country this season, scoring 23, grabbing 12 rebounds and tallying seven assists. “We just kind of got out-toughed and out-physicaled there,” Oats said, “in the beginning of the second half.”Shot blocking highlights tough Michigan defenseThe Crimson Tide loves a corner three, but Michigan seldom gave Alabama any space to make them happen. In fact, the Wolverines not only limited space in the corner, but also blocked several of those attempts from beyond the arc. That was just one way the Wolverines denied shots and limited Alabama’s offense in the second half. Michigan had eight blocks to the Crimson Tide’s one. RECOMMENDEDMichigan entered the game No. 1 in the country in defensive efficiency, per KenPom. The Wolverines showed every bit of it down the stretch as the Crimson Tide averaged a meager .903 points per possession in the second half. “I would say we tried to pretty much get into an offensive match with those guys,” Lendeborg said. “We’re not that kind of team. They’re a way better offensive team than we are. “Once we started slowing the game down, being a lot more physical, and trying to dominate the paint, we started finding more success. Our defense started coming alive, and that really helped us out. It helped our confidence.”
